Front: How does the Java Module System handle reflective access differently from compile-time access?
Back: It enforces separate rules: compile-time access requires exports, while deep reflection requires opens.
Extra: If a package is only exported, reflection tools calling setAccessible(true) on private members will throw InaccessibleObjectException. If it is only opened, the compiler will reject any direct reference to the package.

Front: How does the JVM handle resolution of automatic modules and unnamed modules differently?
Back: Automatic modules can read unnamed modules and other named modules; unnamed modules can read all modules but cannot be required by named modules.
Extra: This asymmetric readability is a key migration feature, ensuring that legacy code on the classpath can still be read by modular code via automatic modules, while preventing named modules from introducing untracked classpath dependencies.

Front: Why do cyclic dependencies in module-info.java fail compile-time validation?
Back: The Java Module System builds a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of modules at startup to ensure safe initialization order. Cycles make this impossible.
Extra: If Module A requires Module B, and Module B requires Module A, javac will reject compilation. Traditional classpath code allowed circular imports between JARs, which often led to brittle, hard-to-maintain codebases.

Front: What error occurs if two different modules contain the same package name (split packages)?
Back: The compiler or JVM startup fails with a split package error.
Extra: Under the module system, a package can belong to only one module to ensure reliable configuration. This guarantees that class-loading is completely deterministic and prevents class shadowing/override security bugs.

Front: What is the consequence of declaring requires transitive instead of a plain requires?
Back: It propagates readability: any module that requires the current module automatically gains readability to the transitively required module.
Extra: Use requires transitive when a module's public API exposes types defined in another module. This avoids requiring downstream users to explicitly declare dependencies on implementation details.

Front: What is the difference between open modules and opening specific packages?
Back: An open module (open module com.foo) opens all its packages for reflection, while opens com.foo.bar opens only that specific package.
Extra: Declaring open module is a shortcut for migration, but it defeats some encapsulation benefits. Opening specific packages is the preferred, more secure approach.
